text: Mid-course test, track one. Good afternoon. Today we're joined by Dr Adam Pearson, Professor of Education. Recent research has revealed several issues around employing and becoming a qualified early years teacher, or EYT. That's a teacher for children up to the age of five, isn't it? Hello, Simona. Yes, children who attend nursery school, and there are some barriers to becoming an EYT. There is a lack of interest among high school graduates to obtain a qualification in this field because it has limited career prospects, and it takes around four years to obtain the early years initial teacher training qualification. This qualification allows graduates to teach children from zero to five years old only. So if they want to teach in schools with older students as their career develops, they will need a further academic qualification. Most importantly, however, once you obtain a qualification in the field, the job is poorly paid, especially when compared to primary or secondary school teachers. A recent survey found that many early years teachers don't receive graduate level pay, with some earning as little as 13,000 pines per year. What is the reason for that? Mainly it's because early years teachers don't get the qualified teacher status, called QTS. The government says both qualifications, the QTS and the EYT, are equal and should therefore receive the same pay. However, employers don't see it that way. Many graduate trainees who go on to acquire EYT status find that whilst they end up with more teaching responsibility, they don't receive the pay and recognition they deserve. The EYT is wrongly viewed as a lesser qualification. Do you think the government is doing enough to increase the number of EYTs? Well, the number of EYTs is declining year after year. As things stand, there are 40% fewer EYTs than the government's target of 2,400. The government has been criticised for this. According to our data, for example, just 595 students enrolled on EYT courses in the academic year 2017-2018, even though EYTs had received financial aid to train. What's your view of the EYT role? Is it easier to teach the under-5s than, say, primary or secondary aged children? That's a complex question to answer. There are a lot of considerations. How the school is run and managed must be considered together with the student behaviour, whether colleagues are professional, etc. I've visited some nursery schools in, for example, poor areas where the EYT has taken on the role of carer and mentor. Others have needed more specific skills in teaching very young children with learning difficulties, for example, dyslexia or autism. Often the schools are underfunded. Although the EYT does not need to specialise in one subject, they need to be skilled in many. We briefly talked about employers. What should they be doing differently? Well, the nursery schools are under pressure and I'll explain why. I mentioned that often they don't have much funding. Obviously many of the children attending nursery are fee-paying. It's not a legal requirement for a child to attend school until the age of four, as you know. Recently, however, the government has introduced 15 hours free childcare per week. That works out at around 7,000 pounds of free nursery care per child. This is great news for parents on lower incomes, but leaves the school with very little to pay its teachers. This is why many are earning little above the minimum wage. Well, unfortunately we've come to the end of the podcast. I'd like to thank Dr Pearson for sharing the results of the research and highlighting just how important early years teachers are. Join me next time for Science in the City.
